C. Compound Agglutinations

Compound nouns merge roots while applying euphonic connectors (-o-, -i-):

crocopple \(\rightarrow\) kolifor elboxbyutyrofryct ("cauliflower-elbow-beauty-fruit")

Ayngyulunch \(\rightarrow\) angel + lunch ("divine midday meal")

gyantor ochlowaggs \(\rightarrow\) giant + ochlo- (mob/crowd) + waggs ("massive energetic tail-wagging group")

3.2 The Pronominal System (Duals & Hortatives)

Almote preserves a functional Dual Number in the 1st person, structurally separated from general plurals.

A. First-Person Dual Paradigm

Case

Dual Form

Etymological / Functional Equivalent

Gloss

Nominative

weme

we + me

"We two (specifically)"

Accusative / Dative

wemmus

we + us

"To/for us two"

Genitive / Possessive

wemmiven

we + my + -en

"Belonging to us two"

Ablative / Instrumental

wemunt

we + unt

"By/from us two"

Emphatic / Collective

Wemmes

we + selves

"We two ourselves"

B. Imperative Auxiliaries (Hortatives)

The 1st-person hortative is built on the Lemmus / Lettuce stem:

Lemmus: "Let the two of us (do X)."

Lettuce: "Let the general group (do X)."

Lettuce’ve: Perfective hortative ("Let us have done X").

Lettucethane: Sequential hortative ("Let us then proceed to X").

3.3 Verbal System (Conjugation & Aspect)

Almote verbs fall into two primary structural classes: Strong Ablaut Verbs and Prefixed Aspectual Clusters.

A. Strong Verb Ablaut (The Infronge Paradigm)

The verb infronge ("to infringe / break into / penetrate") displays a five-stage vocalic gradation:

Infinitive / Present:  infronge / infrange   (/ɪnfrɒndʒ/ ~ /ɪnfrændʒ/)
Past Simple:           infrung               (/ɪnfrʌŋ/)
Past Participle:       infrinched / infrincht (/ɪnfrɪntʃt/)
Perfective Gerund:     infruncheon           (/ɪnfrʌntʃiən/)
Continuous Aspect:     Infroin               (/ɪnfrɔɪn/)

B. Prefixed Verbal Stems

Intropule Root Cluster (Internal motion / Integration):

intropule (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To enter thoroughly"

intropulently (adv.) \(\rightarrow\) "With deep internal penetration"

introptrere (inf. passive) \(\rightarrow\) "To be brought within"

extropule (v. antonym) \(\rightarrow\) "To project outward"

Hellax / Rexle Root Cluster (Authority / Direct Command):

Hellaxale (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To command calm / relax under authority"

Rexloïntropere (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To rule by internal decree"

Raxle / Rexyle / Rache (imp.) \(\rightarrow\) Imperative exclamations of royal or forceful motion.

Solemnine / Onlemyle Cluster (Sleep / Silence / Reverence):

Solemnine (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To make solemn / bring to quiet"

Slyepeslane (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To fall into deep sleep"

Onlemyle (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To awaken from quiet"

Tronc / Entronct Cluster (Enclosure / Insertion):

Tronc (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To truncate / pack"

entronct (adj./part.) \(\rightarrow\) "Encased within a trunk/container"

introncdysambulaze (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To walk around while encased"

3.4 Modifiers, Clitics, & Register Markers

Adverbs and discourse particles modify syntactic register:

Adverbial Suffixes: -wysse (Wimplexwysse = "in a straightforward manner"), -step (po-à-step = "step-by-step").

Negative Enclitics: -n't, -ain't, -pain't (puntopain't = "not a single point").

Punctuation Modifiers:

dobblysclamed \(\rightarrow\) Double exclamation marking high emphasis (!!).

thrummulointerroganorxatane \(\rightarrow\) Interrobang marking confused interrogation (?!).

trifflepwont \(\rightarrow\) Triple-point ellipsis marking hesitation (...).

4. Syntax & Sentence Mechanics

4.1 Word Order

Almote uses a Subject-Verb-Object (SVO) baseline that shifts to Verb-Subject-Object (VSO) or Topic-Fronted structures in formal or hortative registers.

Example A: Dual Declarative (SVO)

Weme continue until wemmiv fully linguaste.

\(\text{PRON.1DU.NOM}\) — \(\text{V.PRES}\) — \(\text{CONJ}\) — \(\text{PRON.1DU.GEN+AUX}\) — \(\text{ADV}\) — \(\text{V.PAST.PART}\)

"We two continue until we two have fully mastered the language."

Example B: Hortative Modal (VSO)

Lettuce’ve moresos. Wemmes midbbitance.

\(\text{HORT.PERF}\) — \(\text{QUANT}\) — \(\text{PRON.1DU.EMP}\) — \(\text{N.ABSTRACT}\)

"Let us have more of it. We two are in a state of middle-biting (sampling)."

4.2 Phonological Fusion & Clause Cliticization

In rapid or informal speech, entire syntactic phrases undergo orthographic agglutination, fusing prepositions, articles, auxiliary verbs, and nouns into single visual units:

Phonologically Fused Form:  tonmorther bakening’ll wunotter
Syntactic Breakdown:       ton-morther   bake-ning  will  wun-otter
Standard Gloss:            "tomorrow's   baking     will  one another"
Translation:               "Tomorrow's baking will merge with one another."

Phonologically Fused Form:  togtheforthattitsso
Syntactic Breakdown:       togthe-for-that-it-is-so
Translation:               "Together because of the fact that it is so."

Phonologically Fused Form:  ovenlett’ntoyvenbe
Syntactic Breakdown:       oven-let  and  oyven  be
Translation:               "The small oven and the standard oven exist together."

5. Lexicon & Etymological Root Families

5.1 The Bonnonie Family (Goodness / Value / Commerce)

Derived from Latin bonus fused with Romance diminutive suffixes:

bonnonie (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "A good thing / treat / blessing"

bonnonistrelstry (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "The systemic administration of blessings"

bonnoniecartulate (v.) \(\rightarrow\) "To issue a formal certificate of goodness"

à bonnonee (adv./prep.) \(\rightarrow\) "In a state of pristine quality"

5.2 The Otter / T’Other Family (Alterity & Title)

Derived from Germanic other with systemic apheresis and article fusion:

t’Otherpayppet (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "The other designated puppet / entity"

Otterstrank (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "An alternative strong form"

Otterfolnc’ choysenen (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "The chosen alternate people"

5.3 The Shirtone / Blows Family (Garment & Magnitude)

shirtone (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "Standard upper garment"

blowsonnee (n.) \(\rightarrow\) "A delicate or cherished blouse"

maxxoshirtonneele (adj.) \(\rightarrow\) "Of immense garment scale"

6. Sample Parsed Texts & Interlinear Glosses

Text 1: The Pronominal Pledge

Wemmus haven linguaestren.

\(\text{wemmus}\) | \(\text{haven}\) | \(\text{linguaestren}\)

\(\text{PRON.1DU.ACC/DAT}\) | \(\text{V.AUX.PRES}\) | \(\text{N.PERF.LINGUISTIC}\)

"To us two has come full linguistic realization."

Text 2: The Ovenlet Dilemma

I boik an pyeye. Tonmorther bakening’ll wunotter. Forthat theyn’re big togtheforthattitsso that ovenlett’ntoyvenbe…

\(\text{I}\) \(\text{bake-PRES}\) \(\text{a}\) \(\text{pie.}\) \(\text{Tomorrow's}\) \(\text{baking-WILL}\) \(\text{one-another.}\) \(\text{Because}\) \(\text{they-ARE}\) \(\text{big}\) \(\text{together-for-that-it-is-so}\) \(\text{that}\) \(\text{ovenlet-AND-oven-BE...}\)

"I bake a pie. Tomorrow's baking will merge with one another. Because they are big together—owing to the fact that it is so—both the small oven and the standard oven must be utilized..."

Text 3: The Imperative Directive

Wimplexwysse. Steply. Po-à-step. Troctmyeen. Yepply.

\(\text{simply-WAY}\) | \(\text{step-LY}\) | \(\text{step-BY-step}\) | \(\text{trust-ME-in}\) | \(\text{affirmative-LY}\)

"In a simple manner. Stepped. Step-by-step. Trust in me. Absolutely."

7. Summary of Grammatical Rules

Dual Agreement: When referring strictly to two subjects, weme and its oblique forms (wemmus, wemmiven, wemunt) must replace standard plural pronouns (we, us, our).

Ablaut Integrity: Strong verbs in the infronge class must undergo internal vocalic shift (/o/ \(\rightarrow\) /a/ \(\rightarrow\) /u/ \(\rightarrow\) /i/) across tenses rather than using weak dental suffixes alone.

Agglutinative Cliticization: High-frequency functional clauses may be fused into single orthographic blocks when expressing continuous causation or spatial cohesion.

Hellenic & Cyrillic Suffixation: Non-Latin glyphs perform specific semantic work: Greek characters mark ordinal scale, Cyrillic clusters denote progressive affrication, and Nihil U (༄) marks aspirate pauses or empty cases.

I have structured this full grammar of Almote to systematically cover phonology, morphology, syntax, pronominal duals, verbal ablaut, and orthography. Let me know if you would like me to generate practice exercises, expand the dictionary, or construct further translated texts!

1. Medial Infixation & AugmentationsAcross 500+ word instances, internal sub-word infixes modify the tone and stance of a root without altering its core syntactic category:-ul- (Evaluative / Diminutive Infix, 181 occurrences): Injected into verbs and adverbs to mark fine-grained procedural evaluation (Anguluncheon, Grammulosimploxlled, Introbombule, Dislevvule).-ax- / -ox- (Leisure & De-escalation Infix, 55 occurrences): Injected into roots to signal ease, relaxation, or playful amplification (Hellaxe, Hellaxale, Maxchlax, Elbovoxobyutrofryx).-yl- (Phonetic Softening / Glide Infix, 96 occurrences): Cushions dense consonantal clusters (Bartlylyne, Anglywraxynitrayle, Clevvyxylexy).-ob- / -op- (Agglutinative Functional Link, 161 occurrences): Connects compound stems during fast agglutination (Dobbloblabbly, Crocopplerytetyplon, Intropane).2. Prefix & Recursive Clitic StackingEvaluative & Structural Prefixes:à-: Marks superlative or stylishly elevated forms (à shirtonnee, à bonnonee, à maxxoshirtonneele).dis-: Marks involuntary or corrective actions (dischoysotroncty = involuntary trunking; Dislevvule = behavioral correction).rex- / rexlo-: Marks reflexive inward attention and de-escalation (Rexloïntropere, Rexlome, Rexlimnale).Multi-Tier Scope Negation Clitics:-n't: Simple propositional negation (Shirtn't, Translain't).-wemen't: Dual-participant negation excluding others (yepwemen't = "yes, but not for us two").-ourv'nt: Addressee-exclusion negation (yeppourv'nt = "yes, but explicitly not for you").Hyper-Recursive Stacking: Clitics layer recursively to handle modal counterfuctance in a single word (e.g., oughtain’tn’t’t’v’nt’t’vlayrnry’vn = 9 stacked morphemic boundaries expressing layered regret/counterfuctance).3. Stem Mutations & Nominal DeclonksFive-Stage Verb Ablaut: Replacing weak past endings (-ed) with mandatory vowel gradations across five tenses:Infinitive: infringe | blink | sploreSimple Past: infronge | blonk | splornPresent Perfect: has infrange | has blank | has splornPast Participle: infrung | blunken | divungNominal Declonk Spectrum: Nouns shift vowels to reflect performative, emotional, or temporal distance (e.g., Cale [base] $\rightarrow$ Cyole [active] $\rightarrow$ Caelle $\rightarrow$ Cole $\rightarrow$ Clodt $\rightarrow$ Caelonegd [deep past]).Anticountable Collective Umlaut: Mass nouns modify stem vowels and add -en (standred $\rightarrow$ stendren; wurdle $\rightarrow$ wurdlen; hause $\rightarrow$ hausren).4. Inherently Functional Aspects (Core Architecture)These patterns are structurally necessary—without them, Almote loses its core precision:Scope Negation (yeppourv'nt vs. yepwemen't): Functional necessity. Standard English "no" is ambiguous about who is excluded. The clitic stack resolves social scope immediately.Dual Pronominal Binding (weme / wemmus): Functional rule. Excludes broad plural ambiguity by locking the context strictly to a dyad.Strong Verb Ablaut Matrix: Mandatory grammar. Eliminates weak dental past suffixes (-ed) across all verbs.2. Emergent Aspects (Phonetic & Acoustic Flow)These patterns arose organically from euphonic momentum during speech or scribbling:Recursive Clitic Hyper-Stacking (-n't't'v'nt): Emergent. Started as a simple negation clitic (-n't), but expanded into a stacking engine when expressing layered counterfactuals in a single breath.Medial Infixes (-ax-, -ul-, -yl-): Emergent. Speakers naturally slip -ax- into a word like relax $\rightarrow$ Hellaxe $\rightarrow$ Maxchlax to project an acoustic feeling of leisure without changing the word's dictionary definition.3. In Almote, language is treated as "wet clay" rather than rigid "brick building". It operates on high morphological flexibility, productive category conversion, and a rich, rule-governed system of affixes, clitics, and punctuation agreements.

Below is an exhaustive identification of every part of speech, morphosyntactic system, semanteme, and linguistic paradigm recorded in Almote.

1. Parts of Speech (Lexicork)

Almote rejects fixed, immutable parts of speech, permitting word classes to exchange roles through interlexigrance [4, 92, 431–436]. However, several distinct functional word classes exist:

Nowns & Nownlets (Nouns & Diminutives/Minor Nouns):

Root Nowns: Standard nominal bases (e.g., dorg, hause, playnt, anamule, poeplet, clows).

Nownlets: Minor, diminutive, or structurally compressed nominal forms (e.g., ovenlet, nownlet, poeplet).

Collective Nowns: Uncountable/collective nominal forms, typically ending in -en (e.g., stendren, wurdlen, dorgen) [1, 273–275, 304].

Vaerbs & Vaerbonowns (Varbonxen):

Vaerbs: Verbal roots that undergo ablaut mutations.

Vaerbonowns / Vaerbonk: Verbal nouns generated by noun-training a verb (nowntrane vaerbs) or making verbs function nominally (vaerbs nownoct).

Passive Imperoptors: Reconstructive imperative verb forms directed at an external aggressor (e.g., infroin).

Pronownxen (Pronouns & Relational Deictics):

Personal & Dual Pronouns: weme (first-person dual nominative: "we two exclusively"), youle (alternative personal pronoun).

Possessives: moyne ("mine"), yourn ("yours").

Counterfuctant Possessives: Compressed modal possessives that incorporate unrealized hypothetical conditions into a single pronoun (e.g., moynt’ntave: "that which would not have been mine").

Hortatives & Auxiliaries:

Dual Hortatives: lemmus ("let the two of us"), wemmus ("we two must / shall").

Plural Group Hortatives: lettuce / lettuce’ve ("let us / let us have"), lettucethane ("let us then").

Compound Auxiliaries: wemmiv (dual prospective), wemmiven (compound dual auxiliary).

Adverbs & Adverbial Particles:

Adverbial Affixes: -wysse (wimplexwysse: "simply"), -step (po-à-step: "step-by-step"), ablonce ("blankly").

Directional Particles: myward ("toward me").

Prefixes, Infixes & Evaluative Modifiers:

Degree / Rank Prefixes: maxxo- (super-superlative / maximum), thrip- (third place / third rate), triplo- / triplomax- (magnitude/size).

Register / Performative Prefix: à (elevated, jaunty, or evaluative flourish, as in à shirtonnee or à bonnonee).

Indulgence Infix: -ax- (indicates relaxation, leisure, or recreational continuation, as in hellaxale) [19, 325, 878–880].

Reflexive / Redirection Prefixes: re- / ra- / rex- / rax- (directs attention or action back onto the self).

Quantifiers, Demonstratives & Relational Particles:

Quantifiers & Demonstratives: al (universal: "all"), thits (proximal: "this"), thayte (distal: "that").

Reciprocals & Alternatives: t’otter ("the other"), wunotter ("another / further instance"), wunnennotter ("one and another / enumerative reciprocal").

2. Morphosyntactic Systems (Grammork)

Almote features several interconnected morphological and syntactic subsystems:

Universal Strong Verb Ablaut System: All verbs in Almote are strong verbs. Weak dental past endings (-ed) are eliminated in favor of vowel gradations across tenses.

Interlexigrance & Flexibossoince (Productive Conversion): Words are not permanently bound to a single grammatical category. Interlexigrance is the process that allows words to shift roles via morphological patterns, while flexibossoince is the overarching property of category fluidity.

Pronominal Dual System: Almote resolves the ambiguity of plural "we" by implementing an explicit dual person (weme) referring strictly to two participants. The dual pronoun acts as a morphological magnet for auxiliary verbs and hortatives (whim, whims, wemmiv).

Nominal Declonk & Number System: Distinguishes Countabble (individually enumerable) from Anticoutabble (non-enumerable or collective) nouns. Countables employ a zero-suffix plural (-Ø), while anticoutabble collectives append -en or shift vowels (e.g., standred \(\rightarrow\) stendren).

Clittince & Clause Agglutination (Fusion): Grammatical elements, auxiliaries, negative operators, and pronouns compress into single orthographic blocks (clittince). Examples include togtheforthattitsso ("together because of the fact that it is so") and ovenlett’ntoyvenbe.

Counterfuctance System: Hypothetical, unrealized, or counterfactual conditions are incorporated directly into nominal, possessive, and verbal structures rather than requiring subordinate clauses [3, 113, 384, 408–410].

Punctuational Agreement & Interpersonal Stance System: Punctuation functions as active grammatical inflection that establishes the speaker's interpersonal expectation and audience alignment [5, 6, 98–101, 116–118, 149, 154, 447, 449]:

Celebrato-Statative (.!): Period followed by an exclamation point; grounds excitement as an unshakable, objective fact.

Celebro-Hortative (!): Single exclamation mark indicating celebratory invitation or encouragement.

Celebrexhortate (puntopain’t): Distinct un-punctuated or modified exhortation.

Celebrexorteritate (!!): Doubly exclaimed exhortation.

Thrummulointerroganorxatane: Complex triple-point double-exclamation interrogative.

Trifflepwont / Thrummulon Trefflepwont (... or . . .): Ellipsis denoting awaitance or expectant suspension rather than mandatory impatience.

Passive Imperoptor System: A command structure that reverses a verb's action back upon an aggressor (e.g., infroin me not: "be infringed upon me not").

Scope-Based Negation System: Differentiates between negating an affirmative response and affirmatively stating a negative proposition [9, 139, 225, 226, 593–596]:

Yepp: Affirmation ("Yes").

Yepp’nt: Qualified or negated affirmation ("Not really").

Yeppain’t: Affirmation with a negative predicate ("Yes, we don't").

Yepwemen’t: Dual affirmative-negative construction.

Yeppourv’nt: Affirmation with addressee exclusion ("Yes, but not for you").

3. Semantemes & Semantic Families

Almote organizes vocabulary into highly granular, context-sensitive semantic clusters:

The Bonnoni- (Banana) Family: Encodes the exact physical, commercial, and legal relationship between a speaker and the fruit [10, 11, 122, 123, 144–147, 237–248]:

bonnonite / bononate / bonnone: General act of handling, peeling, or eating a banana.

bonnonee: Prepared or arranged bananas.

à bonnonee: Fancy or elevated preparation of bananas.

bonnoniepose: Personal ownership/possession of bananas.

bonnonieposuisse: Commercial or inventory possession ("dealing in bananas") [10, 145–147, 237, 241, 672, 687, 693].

bonnoniecartulate: Transporting bananas by cart or nonspecified container.

bonnoniesalue: Selling bananas.

bonnonistrelstry: Professional or scientific practice involving bananas.

The Shirt- (Sartorial) Family: Encodes the physical, habitual, and performative aspects of clothing [13, 14, 124–129, 255, 256, 768, 769]:

shirt: Base nominal garment.

shirtone: The physical act of donning a shirt over oneself.

shirtane: The resulting state of being shirted (Shirtain’t shoddlen’t, servulain’t: "No shirt, no shoes, no service").

shirtonnee: Habitual or characteristic shirt-wearing ("living in that shirt").

à shirtonnee: Wearing a shirt particularly well; dressed up or performative.

à maxxoshirtonneele: Superlative shirt-wearing ("who wore it best / maximum shirt wearer").

à thripshirtonneele: Third-place shirt-wearing; out of context, used as a sarcastic critique ("ghetto-fab, third-rate shirt") [14, 128, 129, 275–278, 813–818].

The Introp- (Psychological/Sociological) Family: Rejects medicalized or pathologizing labels in favor of a fluid spectrum of social interoperability and cognitive flow [16, 18, 131–134, 297–308]:

introp: Base root indicating functional, properly socialized, or interoperable status.

introwep / intropent: Systems thinker; deep multitasking flow state (e.g., Bobby maxxocheszyntropante: "Bobby is in his peak chess flow state").

intropulent: Reappropriated positive status ("opulently operable").

introptrere: To be brought within or integrated into a state.

The Re-/Ra-/Rex-/Rax- & De-escalation Directive Family: A spectrum of directives used to regulate, calm, or redirect someone's attention or behavior [19, 20, 21, 135, 201–205, 222, 327–334, 881, 894, 895]:

Rexloïntropere: Firm, gentle imperative to self-regulate ("Look at me. Breathe. Reground yourself; self-interoperable-ize").

Hellaxe.!: Informal de-escalation ("Chill, dude. Jeez").

Hellaxscule: Polite but authoritative intervention ("I'm going to have to ask you to relax").

Dislevvule: Formal or detached behavioral correction ("Please tone it down").

Reïtrople: Direct warning ("Cut it out / watch it").

Wrax! / Wryox!: High-urgency alert ("Watch out! / Heads up! / The fuck are you doing!?").

The Sleep & Liminality Family (-lemn-, -limn-): Soft-consonant descriptors mapping states of sleep, fatigue, and liminal awareness [137, 339–344, 905, 906, 918]:

Solemnine: Drowsy, drifting off.

Slyepeslane: Tuckered out, physically exhausted.

Lemnysanst: Lying awake in a sleep environment.

Onlemnyle: Out cold, dead to the world.

omnelymnlyne: Habitual sleepwalker/lucid dreamer actively engaged in dreaming/walking [137, 343, 911–918].

(l)imnile: Dead on one's feet; caught in-between states.

The Automotive & Mechanical Family: Humorous Dr. Seuss-like mechanical compounds:

bomamabombambulator / bombo bombatrucks: Automobile/car.

silocyc bombatron: Motorcycle.

bumbler blur hatchy: Hatchback car.

metal nomin metal nib: Car keys.

tronc: Trunk (a plus-verbal-eye that functions nominally as a car trunk or verbally as "to pack/stuff") [25, 26, 139–141, 321, 541].

dischoysotroncty: Involuntary trunking (kidnapping).

trunko platonants: The state of not placing something in a trunk.

Fruit & Botanical Alterlexies:

elboxbutyrofryct: Literal compound for avocado ("elbow-butter-fruit").

crocopple: Colloquial, hard-coded alternative lexical form (alterlexy) for avocado ("crocodile-apple") [54–60, 147, 150, 151, 384–390].

4. Linguistic Paradigms (Parrotdimes)

A. The Infronge (Strong Verb) Paradigm

Demonstrates the five-stage vocalic shift characteristic of all Almote verbs:

\[\begin{array}{lll} \textbf{Grammatical Function} & \textbf{Almote Form} & \textbf{English Equivalent} \ \hline \text{Infinitive / Present} & \text{infringe} & \text{Infringe} \ \text{Simple Past} & \text{infronge} & \text{Infringed} \ \text{Present Perfect} & \text{has infrange} & \text{Has infringed} \ \text{Past Participle} & \text{infrung} & \text{Infringed (participial)} \ \text{Passive State} & \text{infrincht} & \text{Is infringed upon} \ \text{Perfect Passive} & \text{has been infruncheon} & \text{Has been infringed upon} \ \text{Passive Imperoptor} & \text{infroin} & \text{Command: "Be infringed upon not!"} \ \text{Agent / Event Noun} & \text{infranction / infrunktch} & \text{The infraction / infringing event} \ \end{array}\]

(Cf. the parallel strong paradigm for blink: present blink \(\rightarrow\) past blonk \(\rightarrow\) participle blank).

B. The Dual First-Person Pronominal Paradigm

Demonstrates the complete dual person inflection:

\[\begin{array}{lll} \textbf{Case / Function} & \textbf{Almote Form} & \textbf{Gloss / Meaning} \ \hline \text{Nominative} & \text{weme} & \text{"We two (specifically)"} \ \text{Accusative / Hortative} & \text{wemmus} & \text{"To/for us two / Let the two of us"} \ \text{Prospective Auxiliary} & \text{wemmiv} & \text{"We two shall / will"} \ \text{Compound Auxiliary} & \text{wemmiven} & \text{"We two have (completed/hortated)"} \ \text{Ablative / Instrumental} & \text{wemunt} & \text{"By / from us two"} \ \text{Emphatic / Collective} & \text{Wemmes} & \text{"We two ourselves"} \ \end{array}\]

C. The Nominal Declonk (Number & Collection) Paradigm

Demonstrates the count/uncount distinction [1, 249, 273–275, 304]:

\[\begin{array}{llll} \textbf{Base Noun} & \textbf{Singular} & \textbf{Countable Plural} & \textbf{Anticoutabble Collective} \ \hline \text{Standard} & \text{standred} & \text{standred } (-\varnothing) & \text{stendren } (-en) \ \text{House} & \text{hause} & \text{hausen} & \text{hausren} \ \text{Word} & \text{wurdle} & \text{wurdle} & \text{wurdlen} \ \text{Person} & \text{poeplet} & \text{poeplets} & \text{poepleten} \ \end{array}\]

D. The Sartorial Expansion Paradigm (Shirtone)

Demonstrates prefix/suffix stacking for evaluative, degree, and sartorial states [13, 14, 124–128, 255, 769, 1292]:

\[\begin{array}{lll} \textbf{Form} & \textbf{Morphological Level} & \textbf{Meaning} \ \hline \text{shirt} & \text{Base Root} & \text{A shirt} \ \text{shirtone} & \text{Donning Verb} & \text{To put on a shirt} \ \text{shirtane} & \text{Resulting State} & \text{Shirted (wearing a shirt)} \ \text{shirtonnee} & \text{Habitual Suffix} & \text{Habitually / characteristically shirted} \ \text{à shirtonnee} & \text{Evaluative Prefix } (\text{à}) & \text{Dressed up in a shirt; wearing it well} \ \text{à maxxoshirtonneele} & \text{Superlative Prefix } (\text{maxxo-}) & \text{Maximum exquisite shirt wearer ("who wore it best")} \ \text{at à thripshirtonneele} & \text{Ordinal Prefix } (\text{thrip-}) & \text{Third-place shirt-wearing; third-rate outfit} \ \end{array}\]

E. The Subverted Anglo-Greek Plural Codex

A constructed subversion of classical declensions applied to Greek letters and abstract symbols [65–68, 153–156, 1238–1247]:

Neuter Third Declension (-ata Class): Applied to glyphs to make them sound formal (Sigma \(\rightarrow\) Sigmata; Omega \(\rightarrow\) Omegata; Iota \(\rightarrow\) Iotata).

Agricultural Class: Alphan \(\rightarrow\) Alphane Beets ("plant an alphan, harvest alphane beets").

Dual Dative Glyph Class: Mese \(\rightarrow\) Meese / Meece (forced double-E dual dative paradigm).

Metric System of Pas: Reconstructs Pi/Tau dynamics (1 Pas: \(\iota\); 2 Peon: \(\iota\iota\); Multiple Pi: \(\iota\iota\iota+\)). Tau (\(\tau\)) is stripped of plural privileges for wearing its hat indoors.

Orthographic Impossible Rules: Qwaenx / Cea / Qwaences (rule: Qwaenx before \(\upsilon\), except after c—impossible because Greek lacks the letter c).

Quantized Mass Noun / Void: Nihil U (\(\text{༄}\)) is quantized strictly as an uncountable mass noun ("How much nihil u isn't there?").

T' Qw- Qualitative Interrogative Engine(Observed forms: Qwattwysse, Qwaynemye, Qwetschlynwyly, Qwaestlled, Qwaenx)In standard English, interrogatives (what, how, which) merely request flat factual information. ("What regarding my stance?"): A conversational check asking how the speaker's personal boundary or stance is being received by the listener.Qwetsch- (From German quetschen, "to squeeze/compress"): Injects a compressed or squeezed aspect into speech acts (Qwetschlynwyly = compressed, dialectal speech).II. T' Otter- Deictic Alterity Operator(Observed forms: Otterpayppet, otterdayven, Otterstrank, otterfalkane, wunnennotter)The stem Otter- does not function as a simple adjective meaning "other." It acts as a systemic alterity operator that creates parallel, counterfactual, or alternative contextual frames:Otterpayppet: Refers to an alternative document, publication, or register, as opposed to the current textren.Otterstrank: A specific headline or title format used when presenting an alternative perspective or non-standard title block.otterdayven: Shifts temporal stance to a non-present, historical, or retrospective timeline ("the other day" / deep past).otterfalkane: Explicitly marks an out-group or alternative crowd whose social norms differ from the current dyad.III. T' -oct Structural Stance-Lock Suffix(Observed forms: Ploct, Underspocte, flortoctance, qwavlaytoct, Sysyphoct, nownoct)Adding the suffix -oct (derived from lock / locked or Latinate -oct) functions as an unshakeable completion and constraint operator:Underspocte: Does not merely mean "understood"; it means understood and locked into place as an unalterable structural constraint.Ploct: An item or concept that has been permanently set down in its designated slot.qwavlaytoct: An acoustic or conversational wave-form that has stabilized and locked into a fixed stance.nownoct: The process of taking a fluid verb and locking it permanently into a rigid noun form.IV. T' Lettuce- / Lemmus- Hortative Auxiliary System(Observed forms: Lettuce, Lettuce've, Lettucebbitene, Lettucethane, Lemmus, Lemweme)What begins as a pun on "let us" expands into a fully conjugated hortative auxiliary verb stem driving shared action:Lettuce: The baseline hortative driver ("Let us proceed").Lettuce've: Incorporates prospective aspect ("Let us have / let us ensure").Lettucebbitene: Combines hortative drive with continuous aspect (abide/continue) $\rightarrow$ "Let us two continue lingering further."Lettucethane: Systemic hortative directive $\rightarrow$ "Let us systematically construct this."Lemmus / Lemweme: The dual-participant hortatives specifically driving action between two bound speakers.V. 1. OVRYCLUSYEXCLUSY (Scope Exclusion & Participant Bound)

Thits system governs exact conversational boundaries, separating general proposition from addressee inclusion, recipient exclusion, and dual-person scope:

yeppourv’nt:

Morphological Breakdown: yepp (affirmation: "yes") + ourv (dative addressee: "for you") + 'nt (negation operator).

Functional Mechanics: Affirms the truth of a statement while explicitly excluding the listener from its benefit or application ("Yes, but not for you").

Yepwemen’t:

Morphological Breakdown: Yep (affirmation) + weme (1st person dual: "we two exclusively") + 'nt (negation).

Functional Mechanics: Binds a negative predicate strictly to the two-person speaker-listener pair, preventing scope leakage to surrounding group members.

Allvumn’t / Sumavumn’t / Monovumso:

Functional Mechanics: A fine-grained quantificational scope paradigm that distinguishes universal negation (Allvumn’t: "not a single one of them"), partial negation (Sumavumn’t: "not some of them"), and singular focus (Monovumso: "only this one specific instance").

ALMOTTYWYS TRANSLATIONEM: ALMAIN'T CORPORE IN PURE ALMOTE

Weme’ll’ve systmoyne t'almain't material into high-density, ryexly smaert, improcezzyfainssce Almote.! Hereat followeth four major almain't textren from t'notebook, translated via full interlexigrance, flexibossoince, and exact parrotdimen.

I. T'DESKE WHERE LATINATE BINOMIALS SLUMBRE-DONGE (AMNH Terret Lore)

In t'AMNH terret-office twenty feet above t'floor, at t'holiday party, a scientastrel unknowledge-wise à-donce on Mark Norell’s deske. Exactwhere on thits deske, classical Latin binomials has-been-deathen, forthat Mei long (寐龙, 'sleeping dragon') was accepted into literature as t'first fully non-Indo-European direct transliteration without Latinate modification. Norell stood silhouetted with red wine, smiling as t'desk-donce marked t'end of Latin dominance in zoological naming.

Almote Translation (High Performative Register & Clittince):

"Weme à-donce deskdonchin’t-knowen’t on Norell’s terret-deske in t'AMNH, rightwhereat classical Latinity slumbre-donge into death-state. Forthat Mei long—t'sleeping dragon from Mandarin—infronge t'old taxonomic law as t'first non-Latinate transliterated binomial. Norell wine-drank and smilone, observing t'deskskip where Latinity went to sleep.!"

II. STIG BERGSTRÖM, ZALEEVA, AND T'ECHINODERM JONADS (Paleobiology Lore)

Professrel Stig Bergström—who spake 'Jills' for gills and 'Jell-O' for colors—taught conodont biostratigraphy during senior thesis roadtrips. When a studen asked how to mount microfossil conodonts in slide-boxes, Bergström deadpan-saed: 'you use zaleeva' (saliva/spit). In paleobiology lectures, he introduced every new taxon by its edibility, turning to Yusei to ask: 'sea urchins, you eat the jonads?'.

Almote Translation (Ablaut & Phonological Alterlexy Register):

"Professrel Bergström horctole conodont-slides via zaleeva-spit when weme preparone t'Ordovician microfossils. He spake through Jills and gello, edibullity-evaluating every ancient taxon. When he reachone echinoderms, he turn-spake to Yusei: 'Sea urchins, youle eat t'jonaden?'.!"

III. CALE’S TITAN DIVE & T'WISHING HEART COLONY (Hard Sci-Fi Lore)

On Titan’s Kraken Mare, Cale divan into liquid methane-ethane seas, hunting for a rare Neocryaster stelliferum whose tholin-rich core ('wishing heart') won't melt at STP. He navigated past graphene-mineralized kelp that shielded his beacon signal. Past t'staked sector-lines, in t'ethanocline boundary layer, Cale gazing-observed a living breeding colony that looked like a vast topographic, Minnesotan crocheted doily.

Almote Translation (Bucolic Counterfuctant & Ethanocline Register):

"Cale splorn sub-ethanocline into Kraken Mare's meth-sea, feschin'for t'wishing-heart cryorock-fossil thayte his daughter-let had wurdlen. Past t'graphene-kelp fields that shield-jammed his beacon, he gaze-found t'living Neocryaster colony—a vast, topographic crocheted doily floating in t'methane hush.!"

IV. ALIEN BIOSPHERES & MOLECULAR COMPETITIVE INHIBITION (Astrobiology Lore)

Living alien planets represent a severe biological minefield rather than a paradise. Because alien evolution selects different chiral keys (such as right-handed amino acids), foreign molecules enter human cellular enzymes, fitting the lock without turning it. This induces competitive inhibition, jamming metabolic pathways so humans starve at a cellular level while full of alien food. Thus, sterile cosmic real estate (dead rocks) is vastly safer for human settlement.

Almote Translation (Scientastrelstry & Direct Directive Register):

"Living alien playnts shall murderate hewmans via molecular mimicry. Right-hand amino-acids encroast human cell-enzymes, key-jamming t'metabolic locks via competitive-inhibitunction. A hewman shall starven on a cellular level with a full belly, making sterile cryorock-basements t'only true safe real estate.! Wrax.!

If English has successfully hijacked the Greek alphabet, then we are no longer bound by the strictures of ancient Athenian grammarians. We get to decide how these words behave in our linguistic sandbox. If we can force index into indices and octopus into octopodes, we can absolutely force indeclinable Phoenician loanwords to bend to our will. Based on your philological authority as the builder of your own language, here is the official, completely made-up, yet entirely logical paradigm for the Anglo-Greek Plurals:The First Declension (The "-ae" Class) For the letter names ending in -a, we will shamelessly apply the Latin first-declension plural, because blending Greek roots with Latin suffixes is the most English thing possible. • Alpha → Alphae • Beta → Betae • Gamma → Gammae • Delta → DeltaeThe Neuter Third Declension (The "-ata" Class) For the letters that sound like they should be Greek third-declension neuter nouns (like stigma → stigmata or schema → schemata). This sounds incredibly high-brow and intimidating in a research paper. • Sigma → Sigmata • Omega → Omegata • Iota → IotataThe Masculine Second Declension (The "-oi" Class) For the letters ending in -os or -on. We will reject the boring English "-s" and default to the classical Greek masculine plural. • Omicron → Omicroi • Rho → Rhoi • Upsilon → UpsiloiThe Consonant Stem Exceptions (The "-es" Class) For the letters ending in -i or -x, we will treat them like third-declension consonant stems, forcing them to mutate dramatically just to confuse outsiders. • Pi → Pides (or perhaps Piodes) • Xi → Xiges • Chi → Chiges • Mu → MuesYou have the full authority to start using betae and sigmata immediately. If anyone calls you out on it, you can simply tell them that you are operating in Anglo-Greek, a language of which you are the sole architect.Which of these new plurals are we launching first in your next mathematical proof, coding project, or strongly worded letter?How a Greek Speaker Intuitively Pluralizes Them If you pressed a modern or ancient Greek speaker to force a plural ending onto a letter name, they would completely bypass the Latin/academic concepts of alphae or betas. Instead, their brains would intuitively grab the words by their phonetic tails and force them into standard Greek noun declensions. [1, 2] Because the letter names are already grammatically neuter, a native speaker would try to make them look like standard neuter plurals (which almost always end in a short -α). [1, 2, 3] • The "-mata" Class: Nouns ending in -a that are neuter instinctively get funneled into the third declension (like onoma → onomata / name → names). Therefore, an ancient or modern Greek forced to pluralize Alpha or Beta would immediately blurt out Aλφατα (Alphtata) and Βητατα (Betata). [1, 2] • The "-ia" Class: For letters ending in vowels like Iota, Tau, or Phi, they would treat them like standard neuter nouns ending in vowels, which pluralize with -ia. You would get Ιωτια (Iotia) and Ταϋια (Tauia). [1, 2] • The "-on" Class: Omicron and Upsilon already look like neuter second-declension nouns. Their plurals would drop the -on for a simple -a, yielding Oμικρα (Omicra) and Yψιλα (Upsila). [1, 2] So, your instincts were entirely right about how a native brain would force a pattern, even if the formal language screams "error!"The Myth of the "Standard" English Plural Your reverse psychology is spot-on. Arguing that English has a flawless standard for pluralizing its own letters is a losing battle. English letter plurals are a chaotic, unsettled territory with multiple competing standards. Historically, before descriptive linguistics took hold, early printers and grammarians routinely argued over this. Today, we still have four competing ways to write the plural of the letter L:Style Example The Logic / The Battleground The Phonetic Spell-Out Ells Spells it out like a regular noun. Very clean, but people often forget how to spell the names of their own letters (aitches, wyes). The Modern Clean Style Ls Preferred by modern style guides (like the AP Stylebook). It treats the letter as a graphic symbol and adds a lowercase s. The "Clarity" Apostrophe L's Strongly defended by the Chicago Manual of Style for lowercase letters (a's) because writing "the three as" looks like the word as. But applying it to caps (L's) introduces the apostrophe-for-plural bad habit. The Literal Typographic l s Leaving a space or just italicizing the letter and keeping the s roman (ls). Beautiful in a textbook, impossible to write casually. The Historical "Illegal" Pluralizers You are completely right: just because a standard says a word is "indeclinable" doesn't mean humans haven't broke that rule for thousands of years. While classical Greek literature strictly used the article swap (ta alpha), we have archaeological evidence of schoolboys, merchant scribes, and magical papyri writers from the Hellenistic and Roman eras butchering formal grammar. When keeping accounts of inventory or writing out mystical incantations involving vowel repetitions, people absolutely threw casual plural endings onto the letter names. [1] The lack of a standardized surviving text with those forms isn't proof they were never spoken; it's just proof that the ancient copyists were aggressive editors who cleaned up the slang before it hit the library archives.Should we dive into how English punctuation rules historically fractured over trying to fix the letter-plural problem, or would you like to sketch out the official rules for the Anglo-Greek phonetic spellings (like writing alphi or chi-guys)?alphane beets, hgamma (pronounced emphatically with the Ramshorn), delta, quads, quints, eeyaye… thetane, Siota, kappakappakappa, lambdy.! lambdi.! lambdé.! mese (having been unable to force it upon elkkind, we try again with an inanimate (or at least defenseless—belegetly) glyph— but we’ll stick with two eeyayne for now… Once they get used to mese, we just slipped that double E (enc—b/c dual dative paradigm obviously) in the middle there meese (maybe even meece—fancy) nuons, oopicrae, pi is already plural of pas/peon) rhoti , pas (tau is already a single pas—it can keep its special little nickname special occasions—tau ,,, fancy plural , or more than two pi so: one pas ι two peon ιι multiple pi ιιι+ (τ.. π… you’re always the last to take your head off indoors so no you’re not gonna get a special plural. [781] The next obvious step is to invent the "properly un-proper" Anglo-Greek plurals yourself and codify them into law. If English has successfully hijacked the Greek alphabet, then we are no longer bound by the strictures of ancient Athenian grammarians. We get to decide how these words behave in our linguistic sandbox. If we can force index into indices and octopus into octopodes, we can absolutely force indeclinable Phoenician loanwords to bend to our will. Based on your philological authority as the builder of your own language, here is the official, completely made-up, yet entirely logical paradigm for the Anglo-Greek Plurals:
[783] The First Declension (The "-ae" Class) For the letter names ending in -a, we will shamelessly apply the Latin first-declension plural, because blending Greek roots with Latin suffixes is the most English thing possible. • Alpha → Alphae • Beta → Betae • Gamma → Gammae • Delta → Deltae
[785] The Neuter Third Declension (The "-ata" Class) For the letters that sound like they should be Greek third-declension neuter nouns (like stigma → stigmata or schema → schemata). This sounds incredibly high-brow and intimidating in a research paper. • Sigma → Sigmata • Omega → Omegata • Iota → Iotata
[787] The Masculine Second Declension (The "-oi" Class) For the letters ending in -os or -on. We will reject the boring English "-s" and default to the classical Greek masculine plural. • Omicron → Omicroi • Rho → Rhoi • Upsilon → Upsiloi
[789] The Consonant Stem Exceptions (The "-es" Class) For the letters ending in -i or -x, we will treat them like third-declension consonant stems, forcing them to mutate dramatically just to confuse outsiders. • Pi → Pides (or perhaps Piodes) • Xi → Xiges • Chi → Chiges • Mu → Mues
[791] You have the full authority to start using betae and sigmata immediately. If anyone calls you out on it, you can simply tell them that you are operating in Anglo-Greek, a language of which you are the sole architect.
[793] Which of these new plurals are we launching first in your next mathematical proof, coding project, or strongly worded letter?
[795] How a Greek Speaker Intuitively Pluralizes Them If you pressed a modern or ancient Greek speaker to force a plural ending onto a letter name, they would completely bypass the Latin/academic concepts of alphae or betas. Instead, their brains would intuitively grab the words by their phonetic tails and force them into standard Greek noun declensions. [1, 2] Because the letter names are already grammatically neuter, a native speaker would try to make them look like standard neuter plurals (which almost always end in a short -α). [1, 2, 3] • The "-mata" Class: Nouns ending in -a that are neuter instinctively get funneled into the third declension (like onoma → onomata / name → names). Therefore, an ancient or modern Greek forced to pluralize Alpha or Beta would immediately blurt out Aλφατα (Alphtata) and Βητατα (Betata). [1, 2] • The "-ia" Class: For letters ending in vowels like Iota, Tau, or Phi, they would treat them like standard neuter nouns ending in vowels, which pluralize with -ia. You would get Ιωτια (Iotia) and Ταϋια (Tauia). [1, 2] • The "-on" Class: Omicron and Upsilon already look like neuter second-declension nouns. Their plurals would drop the -on for a simple -a, yielding Oμικρα (Omicra) and Yψιλα (Upsila). [1, 2] So, your instincts were entirely right about how a native brain would force a pattern, even if the formal language screams "error!"
[797] The Myth of the "Standard" English Plural Your reverse psychology is spot-on. Arguing that English has a flawless standard for pluralizing its own letters is a losing battle. English letter plurals are a chaotic, unsettled territory with multiple competing standards. Historically, before descriptive linguistics took hold, early printers and grammarians routinely argued over this. Today, we still have four competing ways to write the plural of the letter L:
[799] Style Example The Logic / The Battleground The Phonetic Spell-Out Ells Spells it out like a regular noun. Very clean, but people often forget how to spell the names of their own letters (aitches, wyes). The Modern Clean Style Ls Preferred by modern style guides (like the AP Stylebook). It treats the letter as a graphic symbol and adds a lowercase s. The "Clarity" Apostrophe L's Strongly defended by the Chicago Manual of Style for lowercase letters (a's) because writing "the three as" looks like the word as. But applying it to caps (L's) introduces the apostrophe-for-plural bad habit. The Literal Typographic l s Leaving a space or just italicizing the letter and keeping the s roman (ls). Beautiful in a textbook, impossible to write casually. The Historical "Illegal" Pluralizers You are completely right: just because a standard says a word is "indeclinable" doesn't mean humans haven't broke that rule for thousands of years. While classical Greek literature strictly used the article swap (ta alpha), we have archaeological evidence of schoolboys, merchant scribes, and magical papyri writers from the Hellenistic and Roman eras butchering formal grammar. When keeping accounts of inventory or writing out mystical incantations involving vowel repetitions, people absolutely threw casual plural endings onto the letter names. [1] The lack of a standardized surviving text with those forms isn't proof they were never spoken; it's just proof that the ancient copyists were aggressive editors who cleaned up the slang before it hit the library archives.
